_about: Daily health indicators. Ranges are general adult clinical references used as a starting point. Every entry with "verified": false must be checked by the research team and given a source before submission.

indicators.name: Resting heart rate

camera._note: App rule: a camera reading (fingertip photoplethysmography) needs a signal-quality score of at least 60/100, otherwise it becomes 'Measure again'. Not a clinical threshold.

indicators.whatIs: How many times your heart beats in one minute while you rest.
howToMeasure: Rest seated or strapped in for 5 minutes.
Put on the chest strap or finger sensor.
Stay still and read the value after 30 seconds.

actions.yellow: Rest for 10 minutes, drink water and measure again. If it stays outside the normal range, note it for your next private medical conference.
actions.red: Stop strenuous work, rest and measure again in 5 minutes. If it is still red, tell your crew medical officer and contact the flight surgeon.

indicators.name: Blood pressure
indicators.whatIs: The pressure of blood on your artery walls: the top number when your heart beats, the bottom number between beats.
howToMeasure: Sit or stay strapped in for 5 minutes without talking.
Put the cuff on your upper arm at heart level.
Press start and stay still until it finishes.

actions.yellow: Measure again after 10 minutes of rest. Reduce salt in your next meals and keep your exercise session.
actions.red: Rest and measure again in 5 minutes. If it is still red, tell your crew medical officer and contact the flight surgeon.

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.whatIs: How warm your body core is. A rise can be a sign that your body is fighting an infection.
howToMeasure: Wait 15 minutes after eating, drinking or exercising.
Use the digital thermometer as shown in its card.
Read the value when it beeps.

actions.yellow: Drink water, rest and measure again in one hour. Note any other symptoms such as a sore throat or tiredness.
actions.red: Rest, isolate from shared food areas if possible and tell your crew medical officer. Contact the flight surgeon.

indicators.name: Fasting blood sugar
indicators.whatIs: How much sugar is in your blood before breakfast. Your body uses it for energy.
howToMeasure: Measure in the morning before eating.
Clean your fingertip and use a new lancet.
Put the drop of blood on the strip and read the meter.

actions.yellow: If low, eat a small snack with sugar and measure again in 15 minutes. If high, review your meals and measure again tomorrow.
actions.red: If low, eat fast sugar now and measure again in 15 minutes. If high or still low, tell your crew medical officer and contact the flight surgeon.

indicators.name: Blood oxygen
indicators.whatIs: How much oxygen your blood is carrying. It shows how well your lungs are working and how good the cabin air is.
howToMeasure: Warm your hand and remove any nail polish.
Clip the sensor on your finger.
Keep still and read the value after 30 seconds.

actions.yellow: Breathe slowly for 2 minutes and measure again. Check the cabin carbon dioxide reading on the environment panel.
actions.red: Measure again on another finger. If it is still red, tell your crew medical officer, check the cabin air and contact the flight surgeon.

indicators.name: Sleep
indicators.whatIs: How many hours you slept in your last sleep period. Sleep keeps your attention and mood steady.
howToMeasure: Check the sleep time on your wrist monitor.
Or write down when you fell asleep and woke up.

actions.yellow: Dim the lights one hour before your next sleep period and avoid screens. Use the eye mask and ear plugs.
actions.red: Tell your crew medical officer. Ask mission control whether your schedule allows extra rest before critical tasks.

indicators.name: Mood
indicators.whatIs: How you feel today, from 1 (very bad) to 5 (very good). Long missions far from home can wear down your mood.
howToMeasure: Take a moment to think about how you feel right now.
Pick the face that matches it best.

actions.yellow: Schedule a call with family or friends and do something you enjoy today. Talk to a crewmate.
actions.red: Your mood has been low for several days. Request a private conference with the flight psychologist.

indicators.name: Radiation dose
indicators.whatIs: How much radiation your personal dosimeter recorded since the last reading. Space radiation can damage cells and raise long-term health risks.
howToMeasure: Read the daily total on your personal dosimeter.
Write the value in millisieverts (mSv).

actions.yellow: Your dose is much higher than your usual days. Check the space weather panel. If a solar storm is active, go to the storm shelter.
actions.red: Go to the storm shelter now and tell mission control.

systems.name: Mind & sleep
systems.about: Your brain controls attention, memory and mood. Isolation, noise and changing light cycles can disturb sleep and mood on long missions.

systems.name: Heart & circulation
systems.about: Your heart pumps blood through your body. Without gravity, fluids shift toward your head and your heart does not need to work as hard, so it can lose fitness.

systems.name: Lungs & breathing
systems.about: Your lungs bring oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. The closed cabin air must be kept clean for them to work well.

systems.name: Blood sugar & energy
systems.about: Your body turns food into energy. Diet, sleep and exercise in space all change how your body handles sugar.

systems.name: Whole body & immunity
systems.about: Your immune system fights infections. Radiation, stress and a closed environment can weaken it during missions.

systems.name: Bones & muscle
systems.about: Without gravity, bones and muscles carry less weight and slowly weaken. They are not measured daily: see Future body.
